# How to Help Your Child with Maths Homework Without Doing It for Them

> **In short:** Pick any AI assistant your family is comfortable with (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, or Le Chat all work), ask it to *explain* a maths idea — not solve the problem — then hand the device to your child. You stay close enough to keep things on track, but the AI teaches and your child does the actual thinking.

Picture this: it's 7pm, your child has a stack of fraction problems, and you haven't done long division in fifteen years. The old options were either struggle through it together (and accidentally take over) or wave your hand and say "figure it out." This guide offers a third option — one that builds independence, uses AI as the explainer, and leaves you in the coaching seat instead of the driver's seat.

It works for kids from about age 8 up through high school, and for any maths topic where your child understands the words but not the method. It will NOT replace a real tutor for a child who is significantly behind, and the AI can sometimes get a multi-step problem wrong — that's exactly why your review at the end matters.

## Before you start
- **An AI assistant your family can use.** ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Mistral's Le Chat, and DeepSeek all work for this. The free plan is fine for everyday homework.
- **A phone, tablet, or laptop** that your child can use comfortably for ten minutes at a time.
- **The actual homework sheet or textbook page** open and ready on the table.
- **Roughly 15–20 minutes** for the first session — it gets faster after the routine settles in.
- A quiet spot where your child can think without siblings, pets, or TV competing for attention.

## Step 1 — Pick one AI assistant and open a fresh chat
Open the AI you already use, or try a new one. On a phone, tap the app icon; on a computer, go to the website. Start a brand-new conversation (a "new chat" or "new thread") so the AI has no memory of past questions. You'll see an empty text box, usually with a placeholder like "Ask anything" or "Message…". If you don't see a fresh-chat option right away, look for a button that looks like a pencil, a plus sign, or the words "New chat" near the top of the screen.
💬 Example: type your child's grade level first so the AI knows how to pitch the explanation: "I'm helping a Year 5 student (about age 10). We'll be working on maths together."
You'll know it worked when the AI replies with something like "Got it — happy to help with Year 5 maths. What are we working on?"

## Step 2 — Ask the AI to explain the idea, not solve the problem
In the same chat, type a short request that asks for an *explanation* — not the answer. The wording matters: "explain how to do this" gets a totally different response from "what is the answer." Mention the topic rather than the specific problem, so your child can apply the idea to the whole set. The AI will reply in plain language, often with a small example of its own. If the explanation feels too grown-up or too babyish, add "explain it more simply" or "explain it for an older student."
💬 Example: "Explain how to add fractions with different denominators, like 1/3 + 1/4. Use one example, then ask me a practice question — do NOT give me the answer yet."
You'll know it worked when the AI explains the method step-by-step and ends by asking your child to try one on their own.

## Step 3 — Hand the device over and step back
Now the key move: physically hand the phone or laptop to your child. Sit nearby — at the same table, not across the room — but stop watching their every keystroke. Resist the urge to say "no, do it like this." Their job is to read the explanation, attempt the practice question the AI gave them, and ask the AI follow-up questions in their own words. Your job is to be present without steering. If your child looks stuck after about 90 seconds, ask "what do you think the AI is asking you to do?" — that single question usually unsticks them.
💬 Example: a quiet prompt your child might type: "I tried 2/3 + 1/4 and got 3/7. Is that right? Show me how to check my own answer."
You'll know it worked when your child is doing the typing themselves and you haven't said a maths word in five minutes.

## Step 4 — When they get stuck, let the AI unstick them
If your child is genuinely stuck (not just thinking — really stuck), tell them to ask the AI for a *hint*, not the answer. Most assistants will give a small nudge when you phrase it this way. If they turn to you for help, your best reply is "let's ask the AI" — and let them type the question themselves. This keeps you out of the explainer role and lets the AI do the heavy lifting. If the AI gives a confusing hint, ask it to "show me an even smaller example first," then build back up.
💬 Example: "I'm stuck on question 4. Can you give me a hint, not the full answer? Show me how to start the first step only."
You'll know it worked when your child gets unstuck, types the next line themselves, and solves the problem without ever hearing your voice explain a fraction.

## Step 5 — Check the work together at the end
Once your child has finished the set, ask them to walk you through the answers out loud. Don't redo the work — instead, ask "show me how you got this one" for any answer you're not sure about. If something looks wrong, take the device back to the AI and ask it to check the working: "Here's my child's working — where did the reasoning go off?" The AI can spot the slip; you don't have to. Praise the process, not just the score: "I like how you showed your work here." If your child can't explain how they got an answer, that's a red flag — it likely means they guessed or copied. Don't argue; just mark it together and revisit tomorrow with a fresh chat.
You'll know it worked when your child can explain at least one answer back to you in their own words, in plain English.

## Step 6 — Save the chat and make it a routine
At the end of the session, ask the AI to give your child a 3-question recap of what they learned today (most assistants will do this without any setup). Screenshot or bookmark the chat so you can come back to it tomorrow. Next time, open a fresh chat for a new topic — but paste yesterday's recap in at the top so the AI remembers where your child left off. Over a week or two, this becomes "the homework spot": same time, same place, same routine. If you'd rather not keep chat history (some families prefer this for privacy), skip the screenshot and just write the recap in the back of the homework book instead.
You'll know it worked when your child starts the session themselves without being asked, and maths homework stops being a nightly argument.

## Common mistakes
- **Doing the maths yourself out loud.** It's tempting, but every time you explain a step, you take a learning moment away. Use the AI for explanations; you only handle setup and review.
- **Asking the AI for the final answer.** If the AI hands over a completed problem, your child will copy it. Always phrase requests so the AI teaches the method and gives practice, not solved problems.
- **Trusting the AI's working without checking.** AI assistants sometimes get maths wrong, especially with multi-step problems. The "show me your working" check at the end is what protects against this.
- **Letting the session run for an hour.** Twenty focused minutes beats sixty tired minutes. If your child is hitting a wall, stop and try again tomorrow — frustration is the enemy of learning.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A nightly homework session that ends with your child saying "I did it myself" instead of "you did it for me" — and you actually enjoy sitting with them again.
- **For your work or business:** The same routine works for any topic you don't remember well — Spanish verb conjugations, chemistry formulas, history dates. The pattern is the same: AI explains, child tries, you review.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one subject and one assistant today. Do Steps 1–3 once, even with a problem you both already know the answer to. The muscle memory matters more than the maths.

## Try it now
Pull up one maths problem your child is stuck on, open any AI assistant you already use, and type: "Explain how to do this kind of problem without giving the answer, then give me a similar practice question." Hand the device over. Watch what happens in the next two minutes.
